screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn a practical workflow for finding and fixing performance problems in Unreal Engine. We start with quick, live measurements using Stat commands to see frame rate and thread timing. A common misconception is optimizing without data; we emphasize profiling first, then targeted fixes. By the end you’ll know how to confirm improvements by re-profiling and reading the same metrics again.

screens.title: Using Stat Commands to Triage Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Stat commands are a fast, low-overhead way to triage performance while the game runs. A Stat command runs in the engine console and prints timings you can read immediately. For example, Stat FPS gives an immediate frames-per-second readout. Stat Unit breaks frame time into Game, Draw, G P U, and RHI components so you can see which subsystem dominates. Stat Game shows detailed per-category or per-class costs on the game thread, allowing you to spot heavy Tick costs such as AI or animation. A concrete walkthrough: place several instances of an actor that performs heavy work in Tick, press the console key, and enter Stat Unit. If Game time is much larger than G P U, focus on game-thread work. Then run Stat Game and scan the output for actor or function names with high times. A common misconception is trusting frame rate alone; FPS can fluctuate for many reasons, and a single metric rarely reveals the true bottleneck. Instead, learn to read the breakdown and use it to decide whether to capture a full trace in Session Frontend. Key takeaway: Stat commands answer the question “which subsystem is slow?” and tell you where to invest deeper analysis.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Stat Commands
Stat commands workflow
A short triage sequence to decide whether deeper profiling is needed.
Step 1 — Quick FPS
Run Stat FPS to see framerate. If FPS is low, continue to the next checks to find which subsystem is responsible.
Step 2 — Breakdown
Run Stat Unit to read Game, Draw, and GPU times. A high Game time points to CPU-side logic such as ticks or AI.
Step 3 — Per-class costs
Run Stat Game to list heavy tick consumers. Identify classes or functions with unusually high times.
Key Takeaway

Use Stat commands to answer whether the problem is CPU, GPU, or render pipeline, then capture a trace only when needed.

Terminal examples
~ Stat FPS
~ Stat Unit
~ Stat Game
These commands are low-overhead and are safe to run during reproduction steps. Use them first to avoid unnecessarily large captures.
Common mistake
Optimizing without reading Stat outputs. If you change code blindly, you might not fix the actual bottleneck and could introduce regressions.

screens.title: Capturing and Using Session Frontend
screens.narratorSegment: Session Frontend is the tool you use when Stat commands indicate a subsystem issue and you need a detailed picture. It captures time-sampled data for C P U and G P U, records call stacks, and shows network and memory metrics over time. The capture process is: open Window → Developer Tools → Session Frontend, connect to your running editor or standalone instance, start a capture, reproduce the slow behavior for several seconds, then stop and open the trace. In the UI you will inspect the C P U view to compare Game Thread, Render Thread, and RHI Thread time. Drill down by selecting a time slice and expanding call stacks to find functions with high cumulative time — this is where optimization yields the best returns. A concrete example: capture while several heavy actors are present, then search for AMyPerformanceActor::Tick in the Game Thread profile to confirm it is the hot function. A common misconception is assuming a long function name equals blame; always verify whether the time shown is self-time or inclusive time from child calls. Closing question: after you identify the hot function, which targeted change will you test first — reduce work, throttle frequency, or remove Tick altogether?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Session Frontend
Capture workflow
  1. Open Session Frontend and connect to the running instance.
  2. Start capture, reproduce the scenario for several seconds, then stop.
  3. Open the CPU/GPU views and select a time range to analyze call stacks.
  4. Find functions with high inclusive or self time and note their file and line context.
Key Takeaway

Record a trace only after quick triage. Use call stacks to pick the smallest, highest-cost target for fix to maximize impact.

Example: find AMyPerformanceActor::Tick
CPU View — Game Thread
Time slice selected: 120ms - AMyPerformanceActor::Tick (inclusive 80ms) - FMath::Sin/Cos loops (self 60ms) - Physics tick (self 10ms) - AI tick (self 5ms)
Misconception
Seeing a long inclusive time doesn't always mean the function's body is slow — it may call slow children. Inspect both self and inclusive times before changing the parent function.

screens.title: Cache Locality — Why contiguous data matters
screens.narratorSegment: Cache locality is the principle of arranging related data contiguously in memory so modern CPUs can load it into cache and access it quickly. Caches are small and very fast compared to main memory, so iterating sequentially over contiguous data reduces cache misses and improves throughput. A concrete example from Unreal: iterating a TArray of structs that contain the data you need is often much faster than iterating a TArray of pointers to heap-allocated structs, because the former keeps fields contiguous in memory. Another example: when you have a list of positions to update each frame, storing them in a contiguous array reduces pointer chasing and cache line faults. A common pitfall is to prematurely change data layout for theoretical gains — always measure with a profile. Also, adding more complex memory packing can reduce readability and introduce bugs if you optimize before confirming a bottleneck. The takeaway is simple: favor contiguous containers when a hot loop accesses many objects, and verify the speed change with Stat and Session Frontend so your trade-offs are justified. Cache Locality — Why contiguous data matters means use contiguous data structures for hot loops to reduce cache misses and improve cpu-bound performance.. In practical terms, organize memory so the cpu cache works for you. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Cache Locality
What is cache locality?
Putting related items next to each other in memory so the CPU can fetch useful data in a single cache line.
Concrete example
Iterating TArray<MyStruct> is usually faster than TArray<MyStruct*> because the struct fields are contiguous, reducing pointer chasing.
Pro tip
When profiling, compare self-time before and after data layout changes to confirm the improvement.
Memory layout comparison
// contiguous struct array
TArray<FMyData> DataArray;
for (int32 i = 0; i < DataArray.Num(); ++i)
{
  Process(DataArray[i].Value);
}

// pointer array (less cache-friendly)
TArray<FMyData*> PtrArray;
for (int32 i = 0; i < PtrArray.Num(); ++i)
{
  Process(PtrArray[i]->Value);
}
Pointer indirection increases memory hops. Prefer contiguous storage for hot paths.

screens.title: Reducing Allocations and Object Pooling
screens.narratorSegment: Frequent allocations and deallocations can be expensive at runtime and cause fragmentation. In game loops where objects are spawned repeatedly — for example, projectiles or particle actors — allocating every frame can incur significant overhead. Object pooling is a common remedy: pre-allocate a pool of reusable objects and activate or reset them rather than constructing and destroying repeatedly. A concrete pattern: reserve a pool of actor instances or pooled components, mark unused ones as inactive, and when you need a new instance, pull from the pool and reinitialize it. This reduces runtime allocations and destructor cost, and stabilizes memory usage. Another important tactic is to avoid allocating inside tight loops: prefer stack or pre-allocated buffers, reuse temporary containers, and use TArray. Reserve when you expect growth. A misconception is that smart pointers like MakeShared eliminate cost; they still allocate on the heap. Use pooling and reserved containers for hot code. Key takeaway: reduce allocation frequency where it matters and verify the change with Session Frontend and Stat to confirm lower C P U pressure and fewer GC spikes. Reducing Allocations and Object Pooling means object pooling and reserved containers reduce allocation overhead and stabilize runtime performance in frequently-used systems.. In practical terms, avoid costly new/delete in hot code paths. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reuse instead of recreate
keyIdea.text: Object pooling and reserved containers reduce allocation overhead and stabilize runtime performance in frequently-used systems.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Allocations & Pooling
Why allocations matter
Heap allocations are relatively slow and can fragment memory; avoid doing them in hot loops or per-frame work.
Object pooling pattern
Pre-allocate instances, keep them inactive when not used, and reinitialize from the pool when needed to avoid repeated allocation overhead.
Check after change
Re-run Session Frontend to confirm reduced allocation-related CPU time and steadier memory usage.
Example — conceptual pseudocode
// pool.reserve(100)
for (int i = 0; i < poolSize; ++i)
{
  pool.Emplace(NewProjectile());
}

// reuse
Projectile* p = pool.Acquire();
if (p) p->ResetAndActivate();
This avoids frequent new/delete calls at runtime and keeps allocations predictable.

screens.title: Avoiding Unnecessary Computations & Tick Management
screens.narratorSegment: The Tick function runs every frame when enabled, so putting heavy computations there without need is a common source of slowdown. The principle is: perform work only when necessary. Options include throttling work to every N frames, gating expensive calculations behind conditions, or disabling Tick entirely when the actor's behavior doesn't need per-frame updates. For example, if you have a heavy loop that only needs updating rarely, check the world frame number and run the expensive code only once every ten frames. Alternatively, move the computation to a separate function and call it only when a triggering event occurs. A common misconception is that small calculations are harmless in Tick; multiplied across many actors, even small costs add up and dominate the Game Thread. Concrete guidance: set PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick = false if the actor can be event-driven, or implement a cheap bounding or visibility check and only run heavy work when the actor is relevant. After you apply a change, re-run Stat Unit and Session Frontend to confirm the drop in Game Thread time. The question to keep in mind: could this work be event-driven instead of per-frame?

keyIdea.title: Tick wisely
keyIdea.text: Limit per-frame work by throttling, gating with conditions, or disabling Tick entirely when unnecessary to reduce game-thread cost.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Tick Management
Strategies to reduce Tick cost
  • Throttle to every N frames: do heavy work only occasionally.
  • Gate with conditions: run heavy code only when relevant state is true.
  • Disable Tick: if work is event-driven, turn off per-frame updates altogether.
Common mistake
Assuming that small per-actor costs are negligible. Multiply a small cost by many actors and you get a large game-thread burden.
Example code
// run heavy work every 10 frames
if (GetWorld()->GetFrameNumber() % 10 == 0)
{
  PerformHeavyComputation();
}

// disable tick if not needed
PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = false;
Check whether the computation can be event-driven instead of being scheduled on every frame.

screens.title: Const Correctness and Compiler-Friendly Code
screens.narratorSegment: Const correctness is a simple coding discipline that helps both readability and performance. Mark functions and parameters const when they don't modify state so the compiler can make stronger assumptions and potentially apply optimizations. Using const for local references or parameters communicates intent and helps avoid accidental writes. Another related idea is writing code in a compiler-friendly style: prefer straightforward loops, avoid unnecessary virtual calls in hot paths, and minimize complex aliasing that prevents inlining and optimizations. A concrete example: mark a getter as const so callers and the compiler know it does not alter the object, and prefer passing by const reference rather than by value when the object is expensive to copy. A common misconception is thinking const alone will yield huge speedups; it usually helps the optimizer incrementally and primarily acts as a correctness tool. The real benefit is a combination of clearer intent, fewer accidental mutations, and slightly better optimization opportunities. Verify changes by profiling; const changes are safe and low-risk, so they are a good first pass when cleaning hot code. Const Correctness and Compiler-Friendly Code means make code clearer and slightly more optimizable by using const correctness and avoiding patterns that block compiler optimizations in hot paths.. In practical terms, help the compiler optimize and enforce intent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Const Correctness
Why use const?
It documents intent, prevents accidental mutation, and can enable small compiler optimizations.
Example
Use const references for function parameters that should not be modified to avoid copies and signal intent.
Pro tip
Const is low-cost and low-risk. Apply it broadly and then profile other structural changes if needed.
Code form matters
// prefer const reference when appropriate
void Process(const FVector& Position)
{
  // read-only
}

// avoid unnecessary virtual calls in hot loops
for (...) { FastNonVirtualCall(); }
Small code-style changes can unblock compiler optimizations. Always confirm with a profile.

screens.title: Debugging with Visual Studio / Rider
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging in an IDE is how you move from symptoms to cause by observing program state at runtime. Attach your debugger to the Unreal Editor or a standalone process to set breakpoints and step through code. Use conditional breakpoints to pause only when a specific condition holds, for example when Health is less than zero or when an unexpected index occurs. Step Over executes the current line and moves on, Step Into enters called functions, and Step Out continues until the current function returns. The Watch window allows you to monitor variables as execution progresses, and the Call Stack shows the chain of function calls that led to the current point — this is especially valuable for crashes because it reveals the path to the failure. A concrete action: build in DebugGame Editor configuration, attach to the editor, reproduce the crash, and let the debugger break on the fault to inspect local state and the call stack. A common mistake is using Release builds for interactive debugging; they often strip symbols and inline aggressively, making stepping and variable inspection unreliable. The takeaway is to pick the correct build configuration and use conditional breakpoints to avoid stopping every frame while still catching rare issues.

narration.text: Debugging in an IDE is how you move from symptoms to cause by observing program state at runtime. Attach your debugger to the Unreal Editor or a standalone process to set breakpoints and step through code. Use conditional breakpoints to pause only when a specific condition holds, for example when Health is less than zero or when an unexpected index occurs. Step Over executes the current line and moves on, Step Into enters called functions, and Step Out continues until the current function returns. The Watch window allows you to monitor variables as execution progresses, and the Call Stack shows the chain of function calls that led to the current point — this is especially valuable for crashes because it reveals the path to the failure. A concrete action: build in DebugGame Editor configuration, attach to the editor, reproduce the crash, and let the debugger break on the fault to inspect local state and the call stack. screens.title: UE_LOG and Structured Logging
screens.narratorSegment: UE_LOG is Unreal's structured logging A P I for emitting messages without stopping execution. Use UE_LOG with a log category to produce messages at verbosity levels like Error, Warning, Display, Log, Verbose, and VeryVerbose. For example, UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("My variable value: %f"), MyVariable) prints a warning with the variable's value. Prefer defining custom categories with DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY_STATIC for subsystem-specific filtering. Use Verbose or VeryVerbose when you want detailed output that is hidden by default in high-verbosity settings, which helps avoid log spam in shipping builds. A concrete example is adding a Verbose log inside a rarely failing code path to capture input values and return early if they look invalid. A common mistake is relying only on print-style output scattered through code; structured UE_LOG messages are searchable, filterable, and appear both in the editor Output Log and standalone log files, which makes postmortem analysis easier. Always balance the amount of logging — excessive logs can also impact performance — and remove or lower verbosity once the issue is resolved. The takeaway: use UE_LOG for targeted, leveled diagnostics and filterable context that helps find hard-to-reproduce bugs.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough — Profiling AMyPerformanceActor
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough follows the starter actor that runs many loop iterations in Tick. Begin by placing several instances of AMyPerformanceActor in your level and run the game in the editor. Open the console and run Stat Unit and Stat Game to confirm Game thread time is high and to spot the actor's tick cost. Next, open Session Frontend, connect to the editor, start a capture, reproduce the slowdown for a few seconds, then stop and inspect the Game Thread. Search for AMyPerformanceActor::Tick in the call tree and confirm whether the heavy cost comes from inner math calls. Once identified, try one of three optimization approaches: first, reduce NumIterations to a smaller value and re-profile; second, run the heavy work conditionally every N frames, for example by checking GetFrameNumber() modulo N; third, disable PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick and perform the computation on demand. For debugging, build DebugGame Editor, set a conditional breakpoint inside the loop, and step to examine Result and index variables. A common mistake is not re-profiling after each change. The final step is to re-run Stat Unit and Session Frontend to verify the performance gain and confirm that you have fixed the real bottleneck.

keyIdea.title: Profile → change → re-profile
keyIdea.text: Identify the hot Tick with Stat and Session Frontend, apply a targeted optimization (reduce work, throttle, or disable Tick), and confirm the improvement by re-profiling.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Starter code overview
// MyPerformanceActor.h and .cpp provided in the lab
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) int32 NumIterations = 1000000;

void Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
  float Result = 0.0f;
  for (int32 i = 0; i < NumIterations; ++i)
  {
    Result += FMath::Sin(i * 0.001f) * FMath::Cos(i * 0.002f);
  }
}
Optimization options
  • Reduce NumIterations to a safe lower value for non-critical actors.
  • Throttle: run the heavy loop every N frames using GetFrameNumber() modulo.
  • Disable Tick and compute on demand when triggered by events.
Check your work

After each change, run Stat Unit and capture a short Session Frontend trace to confirm the Game Thread cost has fallen and that you fixed the true hotspot.

screens.title: Key Concepts

Third, C++ optimizations such as cache locality, reducing allocations, and object pooling reduce runtime cost when applied to real bottlenecks. Fourth, manage Tick: throttle it, gate it, or disable it when work can be event-driven. Fifth, use Visual Studio or Rider in DebugGame or Development builds to set conditional breakpoints, step, and inspect the call stack. Sixth, log strategically with UE_LOG and custom categories, choosing verbosity levels to balance detail and noise. Keep profiling, apply a single targeted change, and re-profile to confirm results.

In this lesson you will learn a practical workflow for finding and fixing performance problems in Unreal Engine. We start with quick, live measurements using Stat commands to see frame rate and thread timing. Then you’ll capture detailed traces with Session Frontend so you can drill into the Game, Render, and RHI threads and find the exact functions costing time. You will also apply C++ techniques such as improving cache locality, reducing frequent allocations, and using object pools to avoid costly new and delete cycles. For debugging, you’ll use Visual Studio or Rider to set breakpoints, step through code, and inspect the call stack, and you’ll rely on UE_LOG for structured, filterable messages. A concrete example you will follow is profiling an actor that performs many iterations in Tick, finding its hot function, and then either reducing iterations, throttling work, or disabling Tick when not needed. A common misconception is optimizing without data; we emphasize profiling first, then targeted fixes. By the end you’ll know how to confirm improvements by re-profiling and reading the same metrics again.

By the end of this chapter you will have four reliable skills you can apply immediately. First, you will use Unreal's Stat commands and Session Frontend to identify where time is spent. That means running Stat FPS, Stat Unit, and Stat Game to get a quick read, then capturing a detailed profile in Session Frontend to find the hot functions. Second, you will apply core C++ optimizations such as arranging data for cache locality, reducing frequent allocations, and using object pools. These techniques help reduce C P U and memory overhead without changing game behavior. Third, you will use Visual Studio or Rider to debug C++ in-editor and in standalone builds, using breakpoints, stepping, watch windows, and the call stack so you can see why a crash or bug happens. Fourth, you will implement and use UE_LOG and custom log categories to create structured, filterable logs that help diagnose issues without pausing the game. For each objective you will see a short mnemonic or example, and a verification milestone so you can confirm competency before moving on.

This continuation emphasizes practical checks and common pitfalls so you know how to avoid wasted effort. You will learn to interpret Stat outputs: Stat FPS for frame rate, Stat Unit for game versus render versus G P U timing, and Stat Game for per-class tick costs. You will practice capturing a profile with Session Frontend, connecting to the running editor, recording C P U and G P U data, and drilling into the call stack to find the offending function. You will learn concrete optimization patterns: prefer contiguous arrays of structs over arrays of pointers for better cache locality, use object pooling to reuse frequently spawned objects, and avoid running expensive calculations inside Tick unless profiling shows it is necessary. You will also learn to pick the correct build: use DebugGame or Development Editor when stepping through code; Release strips symbols and prevents meaningful stepping. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a milestone so you can verify your workflow by re-profiling after a targeted change.

Stat commands are a fast, low-overhead way to triage performance while the game runs. A Stat command runs in the engine console and prints timings you can read immediately. For example, Stat FPS gives an immediate frames-per-second readout. Stat Unit breaks frame time into Game, Draw, G P U, and RHI components so you can see which subsystem dominates. Stat Game shows detailed per-category or per-class costs on the game thread, allowing you to spot heavy Tick costs such as AI or animation. A concrete walkthrough: place several instances of an actor that performs heavy work in Tick, press the console key, and enter Stat Unit. If Game time is much larger than G P U, focus on game-thread work. Then run Stat Game and scan the output for actor or function names with high times. A common misconception is trusting frame rate alone; FPS can fluctuate for many reasons, and a single metric rarely reveals the true bottleneck. Instead, learn to read the breakdown and use it to decide whether to capture a full trace in Session Frontend. Key takeaway: Stat commands answer the question “which subsystem is slow?” and tell you where to invest deeper analysis.

Session Frontend is the tool you use when Stat commands indicate a subsystem issue and you need a detailed picture. It captures time-sampled data for C P U and G P U, records call stacks, and shows network and memory metrics over time. The capture process is: open Window → Developer Tools → Session Frontend, connect to your running editor or standalone instance, start a capture, reproduce the slow behavior for several seconds, then stop and open the trace. In the UI you will inspect the C P U view to compare Game Thread, Render Thread, and RHI Thread time. Drill down by selecting a time slice and expanding call stacks to find functions with high cumulative time — this is where optimization yields the best returns. A concrete example: capture while several heavy actors are present, then search for AMyPerformanceActor::Tick in the Game Thread profile to confirm it is the hot function. A common misconception is assuming a long function name equals blame; always verify whether the time shown is self-time or inclusive time from child calls. Closing question: after you identify the hot function, which targeted change will you test first — reduce work, throttle frequency, or remove Tick altogether?

Cache locality is the principle of arranging related data contiguously in memory so modern CPUs can load it into cache and access it quickly. Caches are small and very fast compared to main memory, so iterating sequentially over contiguous data reduces cache misses and improves throughput. A concrete example from Unreal: iterating a TArray of structs that contain the data you need is often much faster than iterating a TArray of pointers to heap-allocated structs, because the former keeps fields contiguous in memory. Another example: when you have a list of positions to update each frame, storing them in a contiguous array reduces pointer chasing and cache line faults. A common pitfall is to prematurely change data layout for theoretical gains — always measure with a profile. Also, adding more complex memory packing can reduce readability and introduce bugs if you optimize before confirming a bottleneck. The takeaway is simple: favor contiguous containers when a hot loop accesses many objects, and verify the speed change with Stat and Session Frontend so your trade-offs are justified. Cache Locality — Why contiguous data matters means use contiguous data structures for hot loops to reduce cache misses and improve cpu-bound performance.. In practical terms, organize memory so the cpu cache works for you. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Frequent allocations and deallocations can be expensive at runtime and cause fragmentation. In game loops where objects are spawned repeatedly — for example, projectiles or particle actors — allocating every frame can incur significant overhead. Object pooling is a common remedy: pre-allocate a pool of reusable objects and activate or reset them rather than constructing and destroying repeatedly. A concrete pattern: reserve a pool of actor instances or pooled components, mark unused ones as inactive, and when you need a new instance, pull from the pool and reinitialize it. This reduces runtime allocations and destructor cost, and stabilizes memory usage. Another important tactic is to avoid allocating inside tight loops: prefer stack or pre-allocated buffers, reuse temporary containers, and use TArray. Reserve when you expect growth. Key takeaway: reduce allocation frequency where it matters and verify the change with Session Frontend and Stat to confirm lower C P U pressure and fewer GC spikes. The Tick function runs every frame when enabled, so putting heavy computations there without need is a common source of slowdown. The principle is: perform work only when necessary. Practicing this loop will make your optimizations safer and more effective, and will help you avoid the common trap of premature optimization or noisy logs that obscure the real problem.
